reveal.text: A sorted list contains job sizes `[1, 3, 4, 7, 10]`. Find two different values that add to `14` using constant extra space. Because the list is sorted, values farther right are larger.
Opposing pointers keep one position at the left end and one at the right end. Their sum tells us which side can be moved without losing a possible answer.

items: `11 < 14`, so move the left pointer right. Keeping `1` cannot help because every other right value is `<= 10`.
`13 < 14`, so move the left pointer right again.

reveal.text: Use opposing pointers when the data is sorted and moving one boundary has a predictable effect on the comparison. Do not use this rule on unsorted values unless you sort first and the problem allows reordering.
Too small → move the left pointer right. Too large → move the right pointer left.
For sorted `[1, 4, 6, 9]` and target `10`, the first check is `1 + 9`. What happens? Answer: `1 + 9 = 10`, so the pair is found.

glossary.definition: A value or pair that could still be the answer.

reveal.text: A mutable array is `[A, X, B, X, C]`, where `X` means deleted. Compact active records to the front in place, keep their original order, and return the new logical length.
A read pointer inspects every item. A write pointer marks the next position where a kept item belongs. The prefix before `write` is always the cleaned output built so far.

annotations.title: Read every position
annotations.explanation: The read pointer visits the original array in order.

annotations.title: Write only kept items
annotations.explanation: Kept records are copied into the next clean position.

reveal.text: Use read/write pointers for stable in-place filtering, deduplication, or compaction. Unlike opposing pointers, both positions usually move left-to-right.
`read` finds the next candidate. `write` owns the next output position.
After compacting `[A, X, B]`, what logical prefix remains? Answer: `[A, B]` with logical length `2`.

reveal.text: A linked chain is `A → B → C → D → B ...`. Each node has one `next` reference. Detect whether the chain contains a cycle using constant extra memory.
Fast/slow cycle detection uses two pointers on the same chain. `slow` moves one link at a time; `fast` moves two. If the chain loops, the faster pointer eventually catches the slower one.

items: The pointers meet, so a cycle exists.

reveal.text: Use this when each state points to at most one next state and you only need cycle detection with O(1) extra memory. A visited set is simpler to reason about when extra memory is acceptable.
No cycle: `fast` reaches the end. Cycle: `fast` eventually meets `slow`.
If `fast` reaches `None`, what does that prove? Answer: The chain does not contain a cycle.

spans.text: The chain does not contain a cycle.

reveal.text: Telemetry readings are `[4, 2, 7, 1]`. Find the largest total among every contiguous block of exactly `3` readings.
A fixed window is a contiguous region with a constant size. Neighboring windows overlap, so reuse the previous total instead of summing the whole block again.

reveal.code:
def max_window_sum(nums, k):
    total = sum(nums[:k])
    best = total
    for right in range(k, len(nums)):
        total += nums[right]
        total -= nums[right - k]
        best = max(best, total)
    return best

annotations.title: Add the new right value
annotations.explanation: The window grows by one item on the right.

annotations.title: Remove the old left value
annotations.explanation: Removing one item keeps the window size equal to k.

reveal.text: Use a fixed window when every candidate range has the same required length, such as every 5-minute block or every `k` items.
Slide by removing the value that leaves and adding the value that enters.
For `[4, 2, 7, 1]` with `k = 3`, what is the largest window sum? Answer: `13`.

reveal.text: All item sizes are non-negative. For `nums = [2, 1, 5, 1, 3, 2]`, keep a contiguous window whose sum is at most `7`. The window may grow or shrink as values are processed.
A variable window changes size. Move the right edge forward to include new values. When the rule becomes invalid, move the left edge forward until the window is valid again.

With non-negative values, moving `right` forward cannot reduce the sum, and moving `left` forward cannot increase it. That makes the repair direction predictable. With positive and negative values mixed together, this sum rule is not generally safe.

Use a variable window when the answer is contiguous and validity can be repaired by moving one boundary forward. Do not assume a sliding-window sum rule works when negative values can reverse the effect of moving a boundary.
Expand right. If the window becomes invalid, shrink left until it is valid again.
If a sum window contains negative values, is `sum > target → always move left` generally safe? Answer: No.

reveal.text: Several problems all mention arrays and contiguous ranges, but they do not need the same method. Choose the method from how the range is defined and what must be queried.
A fixed window keeps an exact size. A variable window changes size to maintain a rule. Prefix sums precompute cumulative totals for repeated arbitrary range-sum queries.

reveal.text: For exact target sums with mixed positive and negative values, a sum can rise or fall when either boundary moves. A prefix-sum lookup is often a better fit than the usual shrink-when-too-large window rule.
First identify whether the problem fixes the range size, lets the range adapt, or asks many independent range queries.
Choose from the range contract, not from the word `array`.
Thousands of arbitrary range-sum queries on one unchanged array: fixed window, variable window, or prefix sums? Answer: Prefix sums.

reveal.text: Maintenance windows are closed intervals: `[[7, 9], [1, 3], [2, 5]]`. Closed means both endpoints are included. Return the minimum set of intervals covering the same time.
An interval has a start and an end. Sorting intervals by start time makes the next possible overlap adjacent to the current merged interval.

Use sort-then-merge when intervals may arrive out of order and the output is their union. If the output needs original conflicting IDs, keep that identity instead of collapsing everything into anonymous ranges.
Sort by start, then compare each next interval with the current merged interval.
For closed `[1, 3]` and `[3, 5]`, do the intervals overlap? Answer: Yes.

reveal.text: A booking system uses half-open times. Booking A is `[10:00, 11:00)` and booking B is `[11:00, 12:00)`. The first booking stops just before 11:00; the second begins at 11:00.
Endpoint rules decide whether touching intervals overlap. `[start, end]` is closed. `[start, end)` is half-open.
Define endpoint semantics before writing merge, conflict, or scheduling comparisons.
Touching boundaries mean different things under closed and half-open contracts.
Under half-open semantics, do `[1, 3)` and `[3, 5)` overlap? Answer: No.

Write the required output before choosing what interval state to discard or preserve.
Same intervals, different output → potentially different algorithm state.
If the output must name the original conflicting bookings, is an anonymous merged union sufficient? Answer: No.
